title: Born Again to a Living Hope
subtitle: 1 Peter 1:1–9
description: A letter to elect exiles opens with blessing: new birth into a living hope, an inheritance that cannot fade, and faith proved more precious than gold.
paragraphs: Some letters arrive carrying a name the whole church already knows. This one opens with it in the first three words: “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ.” No argument for who he is, no list of credentials after the title. The people who received this letter knew the name, and Peter knew they were scattered. He addresses them as “the elect who are exiles of the Dispersion throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia,” five provinces across what is now Turkey, congregations of believers living as foreigners in places that were not their home. His greeting tells them who they are before it tells them anything else: chosen “according to the foreknowledge of God the Father and sanctified by the Spirit for obedience to Jesus Christ and sprinkling by His blood.” Then the blessing that covers them all, wherever the letter found them: “Grace and peace be yours in abundance.” The letter gives no date for itself and names no city where it was written, and the telling will invent neither. It stands in the undated group of this series, and its first concern is not when it was written but who its readers are: elect, exiles, and held.

Before Peter gives a single instruction, he blesses God for what God has already done. “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ!” The reason follows in one long sentence: “By His great mercy He has given us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.” The hope is living because its ground is a resurrection, a man once dead and now alive, not a wish that things might improve. And the new birth comes with an inheritance, described by what cannot happen to it: “an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven for you.” Earthly inheritances rot, get spent, get fought over and lost. This one is kept where none of that reaches it. Nor are the heirs left unguarded while they wait for it. The same sentence says they are the ones “who through faith are shielded by God’s power for the salvation that is ready to be revealed in the last time.” The inheritance is reserved in heaven and the heirs are shielded on earth, and Peter holds both facts together without letting go of either.

That shielding is not an easy life, and the next line refuses to pretend otherwise. “In this you greatly rejoice, though now for a little while you may have had to suffer grief in various trials.” Both halves stand. The rejoicing is real, and so is the grief, and Peter puts a limit on the grief that he does not put on the joy: a little while. The trials also have a purpose, and he reaches for the strongest picture his hearers knew for proving something's worth. The grief is there “so that the proven character of your faith” may come through the testing shown genuine, faith being “more precious than gold, which perishes even though refined by fire.” Gold is refined by fire and still perishes in the end. Faith refined by fire does not. Its testing ends somewhere better than the assay office: it “may result in praise, glory, and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ.” The trials are not said to be good in themselves. They are said to be proving something that will still be standing when Jesus Christ is revealed.

That revealing is still future for the readers, as it was for Peter, and the letter is honest about the strangeness at the center of their faith: they love a man they have never seen. “Though you have not seen Him, you love Him.” Peter had seen him. The exiles in Pontus and Bithynia had not, and the letter does not treat their unseen faith as a weaker kind: “you do not see Him now, you believe in Him and rejoice with an inexpressible and glorious joy.” The joy is inexpressible, beyond the reach of the words available for it, and glorious, already carrying something of the glory it is waiting for. Believing without seeing is not presented as a problem to be solved. In this letter it is the normal shape of the Christian life, lived by people who heard the message, believed it, and loved the one it was about without ever standing in a room with him.

So the opening lesson ends with the goal already arriving before it is fully reached. The believers are, right now, “receiving the goal of your faith, the salvation of your souls.” Not only promised it for the last time, not only hoping toward it from a distance, but receiving it as a present possession while the trials continue and the inheritance stays reserved. That is the ground this letter will build everything on: a people scattered and grieving, and underneath them a mercy that gave them new birth, a hope that lives because Jesus lives, an inheritance that cannot fade, and a guarding power that does not sleep. What this salvation is, and how far back its story reaches, is where Peter turns next.

title: The Salvation Angels Long to See
subtitle: 1 Peter 1:10–12
description: The prophets searched their own words for this salvation and learned they were serving these hearers; even angels long to look into these things.
paragraphs: The opening blessing said the believers were already receiving the goal of their faith, the salvation of their souls. Now Peter steps back and puts that salvation on a much longer timeline than theirs. “Concerning this salvation, the prophets who foretold the grace to come to you searched and investigated carefully.” The prophets of the older Scriptures, the men whose words the hearers read in the scrolls, had spoken of a grace that was not theirs to receive. It was coming to these scattered believers instead, and the prophets knew their own words pointed past their own lifetimes, and they searched them like men reading a map of a country they would not enter.

What they were searching for was specific. They went looking, Peter says, “trying to determine the time and setting to which the Spirit of Christ in them was pointing when He predicted the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow.” The Spirit of Christ was in them, pointing, and the pointers themselves could not see the whole of what they pointed at. Sufferings and glories were both in their words, both real, and the order between them and the distance between them stayed hidden from the men who wrote them down. Peter does not criticize their searching. He honors it. Their careful investigation is presented as faithfulness, and its limit is presented as part of the plan: they were serving people they would never meet.

That is the answer the searching received. “It was revealed to them that they were not serving themselves, but you, when they foretold the things now announced by those who preached the gospel to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven.” The things announced to the exiles in the five provinces are the very things the prophets foretold. The same Holy Spirit who spoke through the prophets preached the gospel to these hearers, sent from heaven, and the hearers are living inside the arrival of what the writers only searched for. Peter sets no boasting in it. The prophets are not diminished and the hearers are not flattered. A relay is simply described: words carried across centuries by men who investigated what they could not see, delivered at last to people who suffer grief in various trials and are told their faith is more precious than gold.

Then Peter adds one line about witnesses higher than prophets. “Even angels long to look into these things.” The verb carries the picture of stooping to look closely, the way the angels in the older stories stoop over the mercy seat. Heaven's messengers, who saw the law given and the prophets sent, lean in over this salvation with a longing of their own, because what has arrived in these small congregations is large enough to hold the attention of heaven. The hearers are not told this to make them proud. They are told it so that they will not treat as small the thing they have received while their neighbors treat them as small. The next movement of the letter turns from what has been given to how the gifted people are to live, and it begins with their minds.

Three verses carry all of this. The whole of the older Scripture's searching, the Spirit's pointing through sufferers and glories, the revelation that the servers were serving others, and the stooping angels are gathered into a single paragraph in the letter itself. Peter spends no more words on it than that. The salvation is that large, he says in effect, and now that you know its size, prepare to live inside it.

title: Set Your Hope Fully
subtitle: 1 Peter 1:13–17
description: Therefore: minds prepared for action, hope set fully, the old passions left behind, and a holy standard with a reverent fear for the stay as foreigners.
paragraphs: The letter turns from gift to conduct, and the turn is marked by one word: therefore. Because of the living hope, the searched-for salvation, and the angels leaning in, the hearers are to get their minds dressed for work. “Therefore prepare your minds for action. Be sober-minded. Set your hope fully on the grace to be given you at the revelation of Jesus Christ.” The first picture is of a man tucking his robe into his belt so he can move without tripping. Hope here is not a mood that drifts over a person. It is a direction the mind sets on purpose, fully, and the place it is set is not the present improved but the revelation of Jesus Christ, the same revealing the trials of the first lesson were already pointed at.

With the mind set, the character follows. “As obedient children, do not conform to the passions of your former ignorance.” The old life had a shape and the new one is not to be pressed back into it. The passions belong to former ignorance, the days before the hearers knew what they now know, and obedience is named as the family likeness of children. Over against the old shape stands one standard, stated in the oldest lawgiving words. “But just as He who called you is holy, so be holy in all you do.” And the ground under it is a direct quotation, given its address by the words “for it is written”: “Be holy, because I am holy.” Holiness in this letter is not withdrawal from the world the exiles live in. It is conduct in all they do, measured against the character of the God who called them, carried into the same towns and households where they are slandered.

The last verse of the section gives the holiness a tone, and the tone is reverent fear. “Since you call on a Father who judges each one’s work impartially, conduct yourselves in reverent fear during your stay as foreigners.” Father and judge stand in one sentence, and Peter keeps both. The one they call on in prayer is the one who judges without partiality, not impressed by wealth, standing, or claimed closeness, weighing each one's work as it is. The hearers' time on earth is called a stay, a foreigner's residence, temporary lodging in a place that is not finally theirs. That is the ground of the fear: not terror of a stranger, but the awe of children who know their Father sees truly and that their stay here is short.

These five verses are the hinge of the letter. Everything before them describes mercy received; everything after them works out what the received mercy looks like in households, marketplaces, courts, and sufferings. The hinge itself is a set mind, a broken conformity, a holy standard, and a reverent fear. What the receiving actually cost is the next thing Peter tells them, and he tells it in the language of a price paid to buy slaves free.

title: Ransomed with Precious Blood
subtitle: 1 Peter 1:18–25
description: Not silver or gold but precious blood: the ransom price, the Lamb known before the foundation of the world, and the word that stands when the grass withers.
paragraphs: Now the price. “For you know that it was not with perishable things such as silver or gold that you were redeemed from the empty way of life you inherited from your forefathers.” Redeemed is a market word, the price paid to free a slave or ransom a captive, and Peter begins by ruling out the usual currencies. Silver and gold are perishable things. They tarnish, they are spent, they die with the economies that mint them, and they could not have paid for this. The thing purchased out of is named just as plainly: the empty way of life handed down from their forefathers, an inheritance of futility passed along like furniture, generation to generation, until the ransom interrupted it.

What paid instead is stated in one line: “but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot.” The lamb language reaches back to the Passover and the sacrifices, animals inspected for defect before they could be offered, and it sets Christ as the offering that passed every inspection. Nor was this a plan made late. “He was known before the foundation of the world, but was revealed in the last times for your sake.” Known before the world was founded, revealed in the last times, and for your sake: the schedule of the whole thing bends toward the scattered exiles reading the letter. Their faith runs through him to God. “Through Him you believe in God, who raised Him from the dead and glorified Him; and so your faith and hope are in God.” The resurrection and the glory stand behind the hope of the first lesson, and both are credited to the same God the hearers now believe in through Christ.

Ransomed people are then told what ransomed people look like, and the first shape of it is love. “Since you have purified your souls by obedience to the truth so that you have a genuine love for your brothers, love one another deeply, from a pure heart.” The genuine love is already theirs; the command is to deepen it. Underneath the command sits the new birth a second time, now with its seed named: “For you have been born again, not of perishable seed, but of imperishable, through the living and enduring word of God.” Perishable silver could not redeem them and perishable seed did not birth them. Both transactions of their salvation were done in imperishable currency.

Peter proves the word's endurance the way this letter loves to prove things, out of the older Scriptures, and here the quotation is Isaiah's. “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flowers of the field; the grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of the Lord stands forever.” Everything fleshly has a season and the season is short. The word that proclaimed the gospel to them has no season. Then Peter closes the quotation onto their own history in one sentence: “And this is the word that was proclaimed to you.” Isaiah's grass and flower, the prophets searching, the Spirit preaching, and these congregations hearing are all one line now. The first chapter ends there, with the word standing and the people born of it, and the next words in the letter tell them what to crave in order to grow.

title: Living Stones
subtitle: 1 Peter 2:1–10
description: Crave the milk, come to the living stone, and be built into a spiritual house: a chosen people, a royal priesthood, once not a people, now God's own.
paragraphs: Growth begins with a clearing of the ground. “Rid yourselves, therefore, of all malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and slander.” Five things to put off like filthy clothes, and they are all sins of the heart that come out in dealings with other people, the poisons of a community rather than the headlines of a court. Against them Peter sets an appetite. “Like newborn babies, crave pure spiritual milk, so that by it you may grow up in your salvation, now that you have tasted that the Lord is good.” The tasting line is an echo of a psalm about tasting and seeing that the Lord is good, and it suits what has just been said: the people born of the imperishable word are infants in the image, craving the milk of the same word, growing up into the salvation they have only begun to receive.

Then the letter's great building picture arrives, and it arrives through approach. “As you come to Him, the living stone, rejected by men but chosen and precious in God’s sight.” Christ is a stone and alive, two things no builder would say of a stone, and his valuation runs opposite to the market's: rejected by men, chosen and precious to God. The believers come to him and find themselves in the same masonry: “you also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house to be a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.” Stones do not place themselves. They are placed, and the house being built out of these exiles is a temple, its priests are the stones themselves, and its sacrifices are spiritual, offered through the living stone they lean on.

Peter proves the picture out of the Scriptures in three stones. From Isaiah: “See, I lay in Zion a stone, a chosen and precious cornerstone; and the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame.” The cornerstone is laid by God himself in Zion, and faith in him ends in honor, never shame. From the psalms: “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” The builders' rejection and God's installation are the same event seen from two sides. From Isaiah again: “A stone of stumbling and a rock of offense.” And Peter explains the stumbling without flinching: “They stumble because they disobey the word,” and then a clause many readers stumble over in its own right, carried here exactly as he writes it, “to this they were appointed.” The letter does not slow down to solve that appointment. It turns instead to the people the appointment was not describing.

“But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, to proclaim the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light.” The titles are Israel's old titles, the words spoken at Sinai over a redeemed slave people, now laid on congregations of exiles scattered through five Roman provinces. Their job description is proclamation, telling out the virtues of the one who called them. And the mercy line from Hosea closes the section: “Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.” Hosea spoke those words over a judged Israel being restored. Peter lays them on people who were once nothing, a not-people, and are now God's own people by mercy alone. The house is built, the priests are named, and the next thing the letter tells them is how a people like that behaves among the nations who watch them.

title: Foreigners and Exiles
subtitle: 1 Peter 2:11–17
description: Foreigners and exiles among the Gentiles: honorable conduct under slander, submission for the Lord's sake, freedom used as servanthood, and four duties in one line.
paragraphs: The building is finished and the people named; now Peter tells them how to live where they actually live. He addresses them by their true address again: “Beloved, I urge you, as foreigners and exiles, to abstain from the desires of the flesh, which war against your soul.” Foreigners and exiles is not an insult the world gave them. It is the identity the letter has been building from its first line, and the first duty of the identity is a refusal, abstaining from fleshly desires that make war on the soul. The war is inward and constant, and the exile's first battlefield is his own wanting.

The second duty faces outward. “Conduct yourselves with such honor among the Gentiles that, though they slander you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day He visits us.” The slander is assumed, not feared. The answer to it is not a defense brief but a visible life, good deeds laid out where the slanderers can watch them over time, until the watchers end up glorifying the God they slandered the believers for serving. Peter aims the conduct at a future day, the day God visits, and asks them to live now in a way that will read correctly then.

Then comes the section of the letter that has argued with readers ever since: submission to the ruling powers. “Submit yourselves for the Lord’s sake to every human institution, whether to the king as the supreme authority, or to governors as those sent by him to punish those who do wrong and to praise those who do right.” The reason given is the Lord's sake, not the institution's worth, and the institution's own job is stated as Peter's hearers would have recognized it: punishing wrong, praising right. The submission has a missionary purpose, stated next. “For it is God’s will that by doing good you should silence the ignorance of foolish men.” Doing good is the silencer. Not argument, not rebellion, not withdrawal: visible goodness that leaves ignorance with nothing left to say.

Freedom is the letter's next word, and Peter handles it carefully because it cuts two ways. “Live in freedom, but do not use your freedom as a cover-up for evil; live as servants of God.” The exiles are free people, and their freedom is immediately bound up again as servanthood. Freedom used as a cover for evil is named as the one abuse to avoid, and the alternative offered is not less freedom but a different allegiance inside it. People owned by God are the only ones in the letter who are truly free, and their freedom shows itself in service rather than license.

The section ends in four short commands that read like a table of duties for the exile's whole world. “Treat everyone with high regard: Love the brotherhood of believers, fear God, honor the king.” Everyone gets high regard. The brotherhood gets love. God gets fear. The king gets honor. Four relationships, four different currencies, none interchangeable, and the king's honor is kept deliberately below the fear owed to God alone. From the civic order Peter turns next to the hardest submission in the letter, the one inside the household of a master who is not merely unbelieving but unjust.

title: He Entrusted Himself
subtitle: 1 Peter 2:18–25
description: Servants under unreasonable masters, unjust suffering commended, and the pattern that grounds it: Christ suffered, made no threats, and entrusted himself to the just Judge.
paragraphs: Now the letter addresses the people with the least power in its world. “Servants, submit yourselves to your masters with all respect, not only to those who are good and gentle, but even to those who are unreasonable.” Servants in these households were slaves and hired hands under another man's roof and authority, and Peter does not divide their duty by the master's character. The unreasonable master, the crooked one, is named outright, and submission is still the word. What follows is not a praise of the injustice. It is a word about the suffering that comes anyway, and what God makes of it.

“For if anyone endures the pain of unjust suffering because he is conscious of God, this is to be commended.” The suffering is called unjust by Peter himself. The servant has done nothing to earn it, and the commendation does not land on the master's conduct but on the servant's endurance, done with God in view. Peter sharpens it by contrast. “How is it to your credit if you are beaten for doing wrong and you endure it? But if you suffer for doing good and you endure it, this is commendable before God.” Endurance after wrongdoing is ordinary. Endurance after goodness, under a crooked hand, with no retaliation, is the thing heaven commends. The letter carries this straight, as written, neither softening the call nor decorating the injustice that makes it necessary.

Then the ground under the whole teaching rises into view, and it is a person. “For to this you were called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, that you should follow in His footsteps.” The servant's suffering is not an accident in a world God lost track of. It is a calling with footprints already in it. Peter quotes Isaiah's servant song over the pattern: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth.” Innocence is the first mark of the footsteps. The second is the refusal to answer in kind. “When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate; when He suffered, He made no threats, but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly.” Jesus under unjust suffering did not file his case with the crowd. He handed it to the just judge and kept walking, and that entrusting is the step the servants are told to step into.

The example then deepens into the saving act itself, and Peter will not let the two come apart. “He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree, so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness.” The pattern to follow is also the price that ransomed them, example and atonement in the same body on the same tree. Isaiah's lines gather around the close: “By His stripes you are healed.” And the last word of the section names what the rescued people had been and what they now are. They had been sheep, in the prophet's words, “like sheep going astray,” and the present fact answers the straying: “but now you have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.” Souls have an overseer now. The straying is past tense. From the servants, the letter turns to the other great household relation, husbands and wives, and speaks to the wives first.

title: Fellow Heirs of the Gracious Gift
subtitle: 1 Peter 3:1–7
description: Wives whose conduct wins without words, beauty that does not fade, children of Sarah who refuse fear, and husbands warned that honor guards their prayers.
paragraphs: The household teaching reaches marriage, and it reaches the wives first, with a mission in view. “Wives, in the same way, submit yourselves to your husbands, so that even if they refuse to believe the word, they will be won over without words by the behavior of their wives.” The winning is by sight, husbands watching a pure and reverent demeanor at close range, day after day. The men in view include men refusing the word outright, and the evangelist Peter assigns to win them is not an argument but a life observed. Words have already been refused. Behavior has not. The phrase “in the same way” ties the wives to the letter's whole pattern, honor inside a house where the faith is not shared, carried the same way the servants carry theirs.

Then adornment, and Peter relocates it. “Your beauty should not come from outward adornment, such as braided hair or gold jewelry or fine clothes, but from the inner disposition of your heart, the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is precious in God’s sight.” The contrast is between beauty that fades, the whole subject of the grass-and-flower verse in the first chapter, and beauty that does not: a gentle and quiet spirit, unfading because it is set in the heart rather than on it. And its price is named by the only appraiser in the letter whose valuation never reverses. It is precious in God's sight, the same phrase the letter used of the living stone, chosen and precious to God while men rejected it.

Peter gives the wives a lineage to stand in. “For this is how the holy women of the past adorned themselves. They put their hope in God and were submissive to their husbands, just as Sarah obeyed Abraham and called him lord. And you are her children if you do what is right and refuse to give way to fear.” Sarah is the exhibit, carried exactly as Peter presents her, her obedience and her “lord” included without editing, and her children are identified not by descent but by conduct: doing right and refusing fear. The promise folds the wives of the five provinces into the oldest family in the story, on the condition of courage. Fear refused is Sarah's likeness, and it runs under the whole letter, where every hearer is being taught to suffer without being shaken.

Then one verse turns the whole section around, because the husbands are addressed with a condition that has teeth. “Husbands, in the same way, treat your wives with consideration as a delicate vessel, and with honor as fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life, so that your prayers will not be hindered.” In the same way: the husbands are inside the same pattern, not above it. Consideration, honor, and an astonishing title for the wife, a fellow heir of the gracious gift of life, an equal inheritor of the same inheritance the letter opened with. And the stake is the husband's own prayer life. Treat her without honor, Peter says, and your prayers hit a ceiling. The section that began with wives under unbelieving husbands ends with believing husbands warned that heaven listens to how they treat the woman beside them.

Seven verses carry the whole teaching, and the letter does not linger or add qualifications to any part of it. It moves next to the whole congregation at once, all of you, and the marks of the common life are harmony, sympathy, brotherly love, tenderness, and humility, with a psalm waiting to be quoted over them.

title: Prepared to Give a Defense
subtitle: 1 Peter 3:8–17
description: Blessing for insult, a psalm for the tongue, honest comfort for sufferers, and a standing readiness: a gentle defense for the hope that is in you.
paragraphs: The teaching now leaves the household pairs and addresses the whole congregation at once. “Finally, all of you, be like-minded and sympathetic, love as brothers, be tenderhearted and humble.” Five marks of the common life, and the fifth is the one this letter keeps returning to, humility, set here as a community garment rather than private virtue. Then the rule of response that governs how these people answer a hostile world. “Do not repay evil with evil or insult with insult, but with blessing, because to this you were called so that you may inherit a blessing.” Blessing for insult is not presented as a tactic. It is a calling, and it carries an inheritance inside it: those who bless are themselves blessed, heirs answering abuse out of their wealth.

Peter grounds the rule in a psalm, and the psalm is Psalm 34, quoted at length the way this letter loves to quote. “Whoever would love life and see good days must keep his tongue from evil and his lips from deceitful speech. He must turn from evil and do good; he must seek peace and pursue it.” Love of life, in the psalm's terms, is not seized but practiced: tongue guarded, evil turned from, good done, peace chased down. Then the watcher's side of it. “For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and His ears are inclined to their prayer. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.” God sees, God hears, and God's face is set two ways at once, toward the righteous in attention and against evildoers in opposition. The exiles slandered by their neighbors are living under eyes that miss none of it.

Comfort follows, but honest comfort. “Who can harm you if you are zealous for what is good? But even if you should suffer for what is right, you are blessed.” Peter asks the question as if the answer were obvious and then immediately concedes the exception, because his readers are the exception. Suffering for righteousness' sake is not treated as a failure of the promise. It is renamed inside it: blessed. With the blessing comes Isaiah's command, quoted as a word for them: “Do not fear what they fear; do not be shaken.” The fears of the surrounding world are not to set the temperature of the church.

The center of the section is a readiness. “But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope that is in you. But respond with gentleness and respect, keeping a clear conscience, so that those who slander you may be put to shame by your good behavior in Christ.” The defense is a legal word, an answer given under questioning, and Peter expects the questions to come precisely because the hope is visible enough to provoke them. The manner is fixed as tightly as the matter: gentleness, respect, a clear conscience. The slanderers are to be shamed not by counterattack but by conduct they cannot honestly describe as evil. And the section closes by setting suffering in its final frame: “For it is better, if it is God’s will, to suffer for doing good than for doing evil.” Better, under God's will, with the alternatives weighed and found wanting. Why the doing-good suffering has this weight is the letter's next subject, and it takes Peter back to Christ himself, who suffered once for all.

title: Once for All, the Righteous for the Unrighteous
subtitle: 1 Peter 3:18–22
description: Christ suffered once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous; the spirits in prison and the eight in the ark; baptism's pledge; and every power subject to him.
paragraphs: Everything the section has said about suffering for doing good now gets its ground stated in one sentence. “For Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God.” Once for all: the suffering is not a repeating pattern his people copy into their own atonement, but a finished act, done by the righteous one in the place of the unrighteous, with a destination: to bring you to God. Then the two halves of his state are set side by side. “He was put to death in the body but made alive in the Spirit.” Death in the body is real and complete, and so is the life in the Spirit, and Peter moves straight from the second half into one of the most argued-over sentences in the whole New Testament.

Then comes the clause readers have argued over ever since: made alive in the Spirit, he is the one “in whom He also went and preached to the spirits in prison who disobeyed long ago when God waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built.” Peter states it and moves on. Who the spirits are, when the preaching happened, and what exactly was preached are questions Christians have answered more than one way for as long as the letter has been read, and the line is carried here whole, exactly as Peter writes it, with no theory built on it. What Peter himself connects it to is plain. The disobedience he names belongs to Noah's generation, the days when God waited patiently while the ark was being built, and the patience of God in those days is the thread he follows into the next verse.

“In the ark a few people, only eight souls, were saved through water.” Eight souls, a few, saved through the very water that judged the world around them. Then Peter draws the line from that water to the water his readers know. “And this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also,” and he immediately guards what he means with his own clarification, carried in pieces because the verse itself carries a break in it: “not the removal of dirt from the body, but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God,” and the ground of it, “through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.” Baptism saves, Peter says, not as a washing of dirt but as a pledge made to God from a clear conscience, and its power is not in the water but in the resurrection it runs through. The telling states that as he states it, the claim and the clarification together, without adding a practice manual or a denominational verdict in either direction.

The passage ends at the throne. The risen Christ is the one “who has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers subject to Him.” The spirits in prison, the patient God, the eight souls, the baptismal pledge, and the subjected powers all stand inside five verses, and Peter leaves them standing together without sorting them into a system. What the readers are meant to carry away is not a diagram. It is the shape of their own position: saved through water like the eight, under a Christ to whom every power in heaven is already subject, in a world where those powers' earthly counterparts still slander them. From that height the letter descends to the daily armory of chapter 4, where suffering in the body becomes a weapon against sin.

title: The End of All Things Is Near
subtitle: 1 Peter 4:1–11
description: Arm yourselves with the resolve of Christ, close the account of the old life, and face the near end with clear minds, deep love, and open houses.
paragraphs: Chapter 4 opens with an arming. “Therefore, since Christ suffered in His body, arm yourselves with the same resolve, because anyone who has suffered in his body is done with sin.” Resolve is a weapon here, the settled mindset of Christ toward suffering taken up by his people as equipment. The logic runs through the body: the person who has suffered in the body has broken with sin's management of his life, and so “he does not live out his remaining time on earth for human passions, but for the will of God.” Remaining time is the phrase to notice. Whatever time is left is treated as a remainder to be spent deliberately, not a stretch to drift through.

The past gets one verse and it is enough. “For you have spent enough time in the past carrying out the same desires as the Gentiles: living in debauchery, lust, drunkenness, orgies, carousing, and detestable idolatry.” Enough time: the account of the old life is closed, not lamented at length. The old companions notice the change and cannot make sense of it. Peter says “they consider it strange of you not to plunge with them into the same flood of reckless indiscretion, and they heap abuse on you.” Strange is the exile's social sentence, the same strangeness the whole letter assumes, and abuse is its sound. But the abusers are not the final speakers in the matter. “But they will have to give an account to Him who is ready to judge the living and the dead.” Ready: the judge is not being prepared. He is prepared.

Then comes the second of the letter's hard lines, stated whole and left as Peter leaves it. “That is why the gospel was preached even to those who are now dead, so that they might be judged as men in the flesh, but live according to God in the spirit.” Peter gives his reason in the same breath as the claim, judged in the flesh like all men, alive in the spirit according to God, and the telling adds no theory about the preaching or its hearers beyond those words. It stands in the letter beside the spirits in prison as the other sentence on which Christians have long disagreed about the mechanics while agreeing on the text, and the text is what this series carries.

The frame for everything remaining is then announced. “The end of all things is near. Therefore be clear-minded and sober, so that you can pray.” Nearness produces not panic but clarity, prayer, and above all love. “Above all, love one another deeply, because love covers over a multitude of sins.” Deep love among the suffering community covers sins the way the letter's own mercy covered the not-a-people. “Show hospitality to one another without complaining.” Open houses, ungrudging. And gifts are treated as trusts: each one received is to be used serving the others, as good stewards of God's varied grace, so that the speaker speaks “as one conveying the words of God” and the server serves with God's strength, “so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.” The section ends in doxology, glory and power forever, as if the nearness of the end can only be answered with praise. The trial that nearness brings is the next subject, and Peter tells them beforehand not to be surprised by it.

title: Do Not Be Surprised at the Fiery Trial
subtitle: 1 Peter 4:12–19
description: Do not be surprised: rejoice in sharing the sufferings of Christ, refuse shame for his name, and entrust your souls to the faithful Creator.
paragraphs: The trial is named before it is explained, and the first word about it is a refusal of surprise. “Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial that has come upon you, as though something strange were happening to you.” Strange is the world's word for the believers; Peter will not let it become the believers' word for their own suffering. The fiery trial connects backward to the first lesson, where faith was refined like gold by fire, and the fire is now arriving as an experience rather than an image. What the hearers are undergoing is presented as the normal weather of the faith, not a malfunction in it.

The prescribed response is joy, aimed carefully. “But rejoice that you share in the sufferings of Christ, so that you may be overjoyed at the revelation of His glory.” The rejoicing is not in pain itself. It is in the sharing: the sufferings are Christ's sufferings, and the people in them are in his company, with overjoy waiting at the same revelation the letter keeps pointing to. Insult gets the same renaming. “If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you.” The Spirit of glory rests on the insulted, present tense, in the middle of the abuse, the same glory that will be revealed later already settling on the ones bearing the name now.

Then a boundary is drawn with complete bluntness. “Indeed, none of you should suffer as a murderer or thief or wrongdoer, or even as a meddler.” Suffering is not automatically honorable, and the letter that commends unjust suffering refuses to bless suffering that is earned, down to the meddler, the small-scale busybody listed without embarrassment beside murderers and thieves. The line runs between suffering for the name and suffering for one's own conduct, and only one side of it carries the commendation: “But if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed, but glorify God that you bear that name.” Christian is the name the world threw at them, and Peter wears it as a title of honor. Shame belongs to the other list, not to this one.

The last movement of the section is the letter's heaviest sentence. “For it is time for judgment to begin with the family of God; and if it begins with us, what will the outcome be for those who disobey the gospel of God?” Judgment beginning with God's own family recasts the fiery trial itself: the fire on the church is the start of a judgment that will not stop with the church, and the question about the disobedient is left hanging with its full weight. Peter quotes Proverbs for the point, in the form the Greek Scriptures carried it: “If it is hard for the righteous to be saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?” Nothing in the section is softened, and the conclusion given to the sufferers is not escape but entrusting, the same verb used of Jesus in the second chapter: “So then, those who suffer according to God’s will should entrust their souls to their faithful Creator and continue to do good.” Entrust to the faithful Creator, and continue doing good. Holding and doing, together, is the whole instruction. What remains of the letter is the last charge, spoken first to the elders, and it ends with a lion, a promise of restoration, and a kiss.

title: The God of All Grace Will Restore You
subtitle: 1 Peter 5:1–14
description: Shepherds who lead by example, humility under the mighty hand of God, a prowling lion resisted together, and the God of all grace who restores: the letter ends in peace.
paragraphs: The last charge goes to the shepherds first, and Peter speaks to them as one of their own. “As a fellow elder, a witness of Christ’s sufferings, and a partaker of the glory to be revealed, I appeal to the elders among you.” Fellow elder, not apostle, is the standing he chooses for this appeal, and his other two titles hold the letter's whole arc in one line: a witness of the sufferings, a partaker of the glory. His charge to them is about manner more than tasks. “Be shepherds of God’s flock that is among you, watching over them not out of compulsion, but willingly, as God would have you; not out of greed, but out of eagerness; not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock.” The flock is God's, the shepherding is willing and eager, and the authority runs by example rather than by lording. Their pay is deferred to the same revelation everything else waits for: “And when the Chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the crown of glory that will never fade away.” An unfading crown, matching the unfading inheritance of the first lesson.

Then humility is handed to everyone, young and old alike. The young are told to submit to their elders, and then the command widens to everyone: “And all of you, clothe yourselves with humility toward one another,” and the reason is the Proverbs line James also quoted in his letter: “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” The command lands as a posture under power: “Humble yourselves, therefore, under God’s mighty hand, so that in due time He may exalt you.” Due time is God's scheduling, not theirs, and inside the humbling sits one of the most loved sentences in the letter: “Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.” All of it, Peter says, onto a God whose care is the stated reason. Anxiety is not told to evaporate. It is told where to be thrown.

Then the enemy is finally named in the open. “Be sober-minded and alert. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.” The sobriety commanded in the first chapter returns at the last, now with its reason visible: there is a prowler, and he hunts the isolated. The resistance is communal as much as personal. “Resist him, standing firm in your faith and in the knowledge that your brothers throughout the world are undergoing the same kinds of suffering.” No congregation suffers a private trial. The same sufferings are running through the whole scattered family, and knowing it is itself a weapon. Then the letter's final promise gathers every thread: “And after you have suffered for a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to His eternal glory in Christ, will Himself restore you, secure you, strengthen you, and establish you.” A little while, the first lesson's limit on grief, and then God himself doing four works on his people, no agent between. “To Him be the power forever and ever. Amen.”

The farewell is brief and warm. “Through Silvanus, whom I regard as a faithful brother, I have written to you briefly, encouraging you and testifying that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it.” The letter names its own errand in one sentence: this is the true grace of God, stand firm in it. The greetings carry the letter's last place name exactly as it is written: “The church in Babylon, chosen together with you, sends you greetings, as does my son Mark.” Babylon stands in the text undeciphered, a chosen church greeting chosen exiles. And the book that began with grace and peace in abundance ends with the kiss and the peace: “Greet one another with a kiss of love. Peace to all of you who are in Christ.” Nothing is added after it. The exiles are left standing in the grace, which is where Peter meant to leave them.
